title: Quickly (Sn 4.14)
hookLine: read it: how to reach peace quickly
tomorrow: where does fear actually start? the next poem has a guess.

lines: TWO READINGS, BOTH WITH A CASE.
cards: Calm in ten minutes. Better sleep by Friday. A whole new you in a weekend.
The ads promise speed, and some of us buy it more than once.
A poem in the chapter of eights is named Quickly, and its questioner asks the Buddha straight out about the state of peace: how does someone see, and become cool, grasping nothing in the world?
Buddhists read the answer in two ways, and both sides have a good case to make.

teach.h: CUT THE ROOT: I AM THE THINKER.
teach.b: The Buddha's answer in Sutta Nipata 4.14 begins with a seeing: cut, by wisdom, the root of all that spinning thought, the notion I am the thinker. Then train, always mindful, to let inner craving go.
And then the poem keeps going, line after line of ordinary life: don't be puffed up by praise, don't sleep too much, don't gossip, don't scheme over food and clothes.

teach.h: STILL LIKE THE MIDDLE OF THE SEA.
teach.b: Be still, it says, like the middle of the sea, where no wave rises. So which part is the quick part? One view, voiced by teachers in the Chan and Zen schools, stresses sudden awakening.

teach.h: SUDDEN: PEACE IS SEEN, NOT BUILT.
teach.b: Their best case: if peace is something you see, it isn't built in installments, and piling up steps can turn into one more thing to grasp. Look, the poem opens on seeing, not on a checklist.
Another view, voiced by Theravada teachers, stresses gradual training.
Their best case: in another sutta the Buddha says the great ocean slopes down gradually, with no sudden cliff, and so does this training.
And look, the poem doesn't stop at the seeing; it spends line after line on how you eat, sleep and talk. Neither reading has to lose for the poem to make sense, because the poem itself holds both.
A seeing that can come quickly, and a daily life that keeps it, quietly.

how: Chan and Zen teachers often speak of sudden awakening while keeping daily sitting and work practice; Theravada teachers often describe a gradual training of conduct, meditation and wisdom. Both read poems like this one aloud and slowly.

o: the name of a monk who woke up in a single night
a poem on reaching peace, by seeing and by daily conduct
a short teaching on how to meditate faster each day

s: a poem called Quickly must promise instant results with no practice
it opens on a seeing, then spends line after line on how to eat, sleep and talk.
Buddhist schools differ on whether awakening is sudden or gradual
Chan and Zen teachers stress the sudden; Theravada teachers stress gradual training. the poem holds both.

games.q: your friend leans gradual: practice is built step by step. she asks you to make the best case for the sudden side. what do you say?
o: if peace is something you see, piling up steps can become one more thing to grasp.
steps are slow and dull, so it's better to wait for a big moment to come.
the Buddha gave no instructions for daily life, only one flash of insight.
games.why: that's the sudden side at its strongest, and the poem opens on a seeing. the gradual side has its own: the ocean slopes slowly, and the poem goes on, line after line, about daily conduct.

practice: If there's paper near you, write one line by hand, slowly: still, like the middle of the sea, where no wave rises.
Then put the pen down and breathe with the words in front of you, letting each breath be one small wave that rises, comes in, and settles back into the sea.

wordCard.voice: Quickly: the title of Sutta Nipata 4.14, a poem on the state of peace. It opens with a sudden seeing and spends its length on quiet daily conduct.

orig.note: Pali: the spinning out of thought. The poem says to cut its root, 'I am the thinker'.

carryVoice: The line for today: quickly, quietly, the seeing and the keeping of it. Fourteen poems of the eights behind you.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.19 (Paharada Sutta: the ocean slopes gradually, so does the training)
Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (the sudden teaching)
